d1a6ef15b6.q: What are typical starting salaries for architects today?
d1a6ef15b6.a: According to Rob's friend who is a partner at a firm in the Boston area, they are paying students still in school about $20 an hour, and when they graduate…
d1a6ef15b6.e: Architect Career: Salary, Training & What the Job Is Really Like
f: Starting architects in Boston earn around $20 per hour while still in school, rising to approximately $25 per hour once they graduate. Entry-level compensation is notoriously low across the profession, but salary varies significantly by geography—you earn less in Texas than in major markets like Boston, New York, or Los Angeles. The payoff comes later: if you persist and eventually own your own firm, the financial picture transforms dramatically.

The early years of an architecture career demand patience and genuine passion for the work. Low starting pay is an industry standard , particularly for unlicensed graduates completing their apprenticeship hours toward full licensure. As one Boston-area architecture firm partner noted, the hourly wage reflects the training period—students and recent graduates are still building their expertise under supervision, which limits immediate earning power.

Geography plays a decisive role in compensation. Regional cost of living and market demand directly influence what firms can and will pay. Markets like Boston, New York, and Los Angeles command higher salaries due to competition for talent and higher project costs, while markets like Texas offer lower entry-level wages. This geographic disparity persists throughout an architect's early career before narrowing as experience and credentials accumulate.

Rob Dupont, whose career spans over 40 years and includes establishing his own practice, emphasizes the long-term trajectory. As he explains in the episode , the low initial salary is survivable only if you have genuine love for the profession—otherwise, the financial sacrifice early on will wear you down.
From apprentice wages to firm ownership

The shift in earning potential happens when architects transition from employees to business owners. Ownership of your own firm fundamentally changes the financial dynamic: instead of earning an hourly wage or modest annual salary, you capture project fees, build client relationships, and control your revenue stream. This progression from $20–25 per hour as a new graduate to potentially six-figure income as a principal is the real economic story of the profession.

5021586e47.q: How does owning your own architecture firm change earning potential compared to working for others?
5021586e47.a: Having your own firm makes a big difference in how much money you can make. Rob's partner in Boston who specializes in building envelope and is a partner at…
5021586e47.e: Architect Career: Salary, Training & What the Job Is Really Like
f: Owning your own architecture firm creates a dramatic jump in earning potential — partners at established firms can make six figures, while starting salaries for new architects hover around $25 per hour. The gap reflects not just seniority, but the fundamental shift from earning an hourly wage to building equity and capturing the full value of your work through client relationships and ongoing business growth.
From Employment to Ownership: The Economic Turning Point

When you work for another firm, your earnings are capped by salary structure and market rates. Entry-level architects in the Boston area today earn approximately $25 per hour—a wage that barely breaks $50,000 annually for full-time work. In contrast, Rob Dupont explains in the podcast , his partner in Boston who specializes in building envelope and holds an ownership stake at their firm is earning six figures.

Rob's own transition illustrates this shift. He started his career as an apprentice under architect Robert Young in Kingston, building foundational skills while earning an employee's wage. But around 1991–1992, during an economic slowdown, he was let go from his position. Rather than seeking another firm job, he made a deliberate choice: he began leveraging his network to generate his own projects and build his own business. That decision transformed his economic trajectory entirely.
Networking as the Bridge to Six-Figure Potential

The leap from $25/hour to six figures doesn't happen overnight, and it doesn't happen in isolation. Over his 40+ years practicing architecture, Rob built deep relationships with builders, engineers, contractors, and past clients. Those connections became the engine of his business. As discussed at length in this podcast , the architect who owns the firm doesn't just earn a salary—they earn referral fees, repeat business, and the compounding value of a reputation built over decades.

ba77f7d61a.q: How do you work with builders and contractors to ensure successful project outcomes?
ba77f7d61a.a: Rob gets a lot of referrals from builders because he knows how to build a building well. He creates detailed plans that make the builder's work easier,…
ba77f7d61a.e: Architect Career: Salary, Training & What the Job Is Really Like
f: Successful collaboration with builders starts with detailed plans that make the builder's work easier , reducing friction and miscommunication before it starts. Rob Dupont frames this as a three-legged stool: the architect, builder, and owner all support one another equally, and this mutual respect and clear communication deliver a successful product.

Getting consistent referrals from builders isn't accidental—it reflects a deeper professional philosophy. When an architect delivers plans that are thorough and buildable, contractors don't have to improvise or interpret ambiguities on site. This eliminates one of the largest sources of conflict in construction: the gap between what was designed and what can actually be built.
The Three-Legged Stool: A Foundation for Trust

Rob Dupont describes his approach to project partnerships using a simple metaphor. Each party—architect, builder, and owner—bears equal weight in the relationship. When any one leg weakens, the entire structure fails. This isn't a hierarchy where the architect dictates and the builder obeys; it's a balanced system where each role is respected and interdependent.

The architect's job is to understand what the owner wants and translate it into documents the builder can execute. The builder brings real-world expertise about what's feasible, cost-effective, and buildable. The owner articulates their vision and constraints. When these three parties communicate clearly and trust each other's expertise, as Rob explains in the episode , the friction that derails so many projects simply evaporates.

This balanced approach is why Rob has built extensive networks with builders and contractors throughout his 40+ years of practice. Builders refer him work because they know his plans will be clear, his thinking will be sound, and the project won't become a battlefield between design and construction.

d7b5024b40.q: How much time do architects spend on design versus regulatory and administrative tasks?
d7b5024b40.a: Rob says the vast bulk of time is spent in drawing and construction document drafting in the computer and construction document phase, because there is so…
d7b5024b40.e: Architect Career: Salary, Training & What the Job Is Really Like
f: The vast bulk of an architect's time goes into construction document drafting and regulatory work, not conceptual design. Designs come relatively easily after years of experience, but the documentation phase—packing the drawings with all required information, codes, and specifications—is where the majority of the work truly happens.
The documentation burden eclipses design

Once an architect has accumulated years of practice, the actual creative design phase becomes comparatively straightforward. The real challenge emerges in the construction document and regulatory phase , where enormous amounts of technical information must be compiled, verified, and communicated to builders, engineers, inspectors, and contractors.

This documentation work is not optional padding—it is legally and functionally essential. Building codes, energy conservation requirements, material specifications, structural details, accessibility compliance, and site conditions all demand precise notation. As Rob Dupont explains in the episode , the sheer volume of information that must be inserted into construction documents is what drives the time commitment.

An architect cannot simply hand off a beautiful conceptual sketch to a builder. Every line, dimension, material call-out, and detail must be explicit and complete enough that construction can proceed without ambiguity. This level of precision and completeness is what absorbs the majority of billable and project hours , far more than the initial design concept itself.

Understanding this reality is critical for anyone considering an architecture career: the work is not primarily about creating visionary designs, but about translating those visions into exhaustively documented, legally compliant, and constructable blueprints. Those curious about the specific tools and workflows architects use to manage this documentation can learn more in Rob Dupont's full conversation on Listenly , where he discusses the computer-assisted design process and the practical realities of the profession.

a4e4f76302.q: How much can a stage manager earn on Broadway versus other theater venues?
a4e4f76302.a: On Broadway, the union minimum contract for a production stage manager is $4,000 a week. If working on a hit show like Book of Mormon, Wicked, or Hamilton,…
a4e4f76302.e: Behind the Scenes on Broadway: What a Stage Manager Really Does
f: On Broadway, the union minimum contract for a production stage manager is $4,000 per week . If you land a hit show like Book of Mormon, Wicked, or Hamilton, you can earn $200,000 a year plus pension contributions, health insurance, and retirement benefits. Regional theaters, off-Broadway venues, and smaller productions pay roughly a quarter of Broadway rates, while freelance gigs can be as low as $1,000 for four weeks of work.
The Broadway premium and beyond

The gap between Broadway and other theater sectors is substantial. A stage manager on Broadway benefits from union protections that lock in baseline pay and benefits, whereas regional and off-Broadway stage managers have far fewer guarantees. Hit productions on Broadway can double or triple baseline earnings depending on the show's commercial success and box office performance.

When you're managing a complex production—whether it's the intricate set changes in Hello Dolly or the technical demands of a Broadway musical—the union structure ensures compensation reflects the scale of responsibility. As Billy details in the episode , even what might look like glamorous work requires serious logistical coordination behind the scenes.
Where the money drops off

Regional and off-Broadway venues typically pay one-quarter of Broadway salaries , which can mean $1,000 to $1,500 per week instead of $4,000. Freelance stage management—common for smaller productions, touring shows, or acting class readings—often pays flat project fees rather than weekly rates, sometimes yielding only $1,000 for four weeks of rehearsals and performances combined.

d909ecaa72.q: What does a doula do during pregnancy and childbirth?
d909ecaa72.a: A doula provides a combination of physical and emotional support, helping people advocate for themselves within hospital situations or home births. The doula works with the mother and partner from an initial meeting onwards, offering guidance on appointments, medical questions, and teaching how to communicate effectively with healthcare providers. The doula stays with clients throughout labor—sometimes 10 to 50 hours depending on the birth—and provides continuous presence and advocacy that hospital nurses cannot offer due to their multiple patients and charting responsibilities.
d909ecaa72.e: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula
f: A doula provides physical and emotional support throughout labor and delivery , helping people advocate for themselves in hospital or home birth settings. The doula begins working with clients at an initial meeting, guiding them through medical appointments and teaching them how to communicate with healthcare providers. Most importantly, a doula stays continuously present during labor—anywhere from 10 to 50 hours depending on the birth —offering the kind of undivided attention and advocacy that hospital nurses cannot provide due to their multiple patients and charting duties.
Building trust before labor begins

The doula relationship starts well before active labor. As Mary Riley explains in her episode , a doula meets with the pregnant person and their partner during initial consultations to understand their values, fears, and hopes for the birth. This early connection allows the doula to tailor their support to what each family actually needs—whether that's help navigating hospital systems, clarifying medical jargon, or advocating for specific preferences.

During pregnancy, the doula helps clients prepare mentally and emotionally , often teaching communication techniques they can use when speaking with doctors and nurses. The goal is not to make medical decisions for the client, but to ensure they feel informed, heard, and empowered to make their own choices within whatever birth setting they choose.
The continuous presence through labor

Once labor begins, the doula becomes a constant, non-medical presence. Unlike hospital staff who rotate shifts and juggle multiple patients, a doula stays with one family for the entire labor—sometimes spanning 10 to 50 hours . This continuity matters enormously because labor is unpredictable; what a client needs at hour 3 of labor is very different from what they need at hour 20.

67d275ee99.q: What certification and training is required to become a doula?
67d275ee99.a: Doula certification typically involves one or two weekend workshops, book learning, and tests with practice. Nowadays the process is somewhat more involved. Certification must be renewed annually. There are no rigid medical prerequisites, and the focus is on building skills through hands-on experience with births rather than formal medical education.
67d275ee99.e: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula
f: Doula certification typically involves one or two weekend workshops combined with book learning and practical testing , though the process has become more involved in recent years. Certification must be renewed annually, and there are no rigid medical prerequisites—the focus centers on building hands-on skills through actual birth experience rather than formal medical education.

The path to becoming a doula is remarkably accessible. Unlike many healthcare professions, there is no mandatory medical background required to start the certification process. This approach reflects the core of doula work: learning directly from births themselves rather than through classroom theory alone.

As Mary Riley explains in the episode , the training framework centers on practical competency. You attend concentrated weekend workshops, complete assigned reading, and then demonstrate your knowledge through testing before moving forward.
Annual renewal and continuous skill development

The certification process does not end once you complete initial training. Annual renewal is mandatory to maintain your credential as a practicing doula. This ongoing requirement ensures that doulas stay current and continue refining their approach to birth support.

Beyond the formal certification structure, the real education happens on the job. Mary Riley notes in her conversation with Mirav Ozeri that you develop skills by responding to the unique needs of each birth—no two are identical. The hands-on experience with actual births becomes your greatest teacher, far more influential than any single textbook or workshop alone.

69b1bc11bd.q: How much can a beginning doula earn, and what is the typical fee range by experience level?
69b1bc11bd.a: Beginning doulas might charge a few hundred dollars, primarily to cover costs like childcare and gas, or even do births for free to gain education. As experience grows, doulas in rural and suburban areas outside major cities typically earn between $1,500 to a couple thousand dollars per birth. In New York City, doulas can charge $3,000 to $4,000 per birth, though Mary Riley does not work in the city.
69b1bc11bd.e: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula
f: Beginning doulas typically earn a few hundred dollars per birth , often used to cover basic costs like childcare and gas, while experienced doulas in rural and suburban areas charge $1,500 to $2,000+ per birth. In major cities like New York City, doulas can command $3,000 to $4,000 per birth, reflecting significant variation based on location and experience.

When starting out, many doulas accept lower fees or even work for free to build experience and establish their practice. As discussed in the episode , these early births are critical learning opportunities that help new practitioners refine their skills and grow confidence in their work.

The jump from beginner to experienced doula represents a substantial income increase. Those working outside major metropolitan areas can realistically expect to earn $1,500 to a couple thousand dollars per birth once they've built a solid reputation and client base. This typically reflects 2–5 years of consistent practice and positive client feedback.

Urban markets, particularly high-cost-of-living areas, reward expertise and established credentials with significantly higher rates. Mary Riley, who has supported over 2,500 births , notes that while New York City doulas regularly charge $3,000 to $4,000 per birth, geography remains one of the strongest determinants of earning potential in this field.

Location matters as much as experience. A beginning doula in a small town or suburban area will earn far less than even a moderately experienced doula in a major city, even if both are equally skilled. The podcast explores how doulas in different regions structure their pricing and build sustainable careers within their local markets.
"They have to walk away from this birth looking at each other and hopefully say, look at what we did together, because we have to parent and raise this child for the rest of our lives."

012b81b0c8.a: Mary Riley meets with the mother, partner, and any family members who will be present, and once everyone is comfortable with each other, the doula begins support. f: A doula typically begins working after an initial meeting where the mother, partner, and any family members who will be present get to know each other . Once everyone feels comfortable, the relationship officially starts. Most clients see their doula two or three more times during pregnancy, with ongoing contact via phone calls and texts during appointments, ultrasounds, or whenever questions arise.

The timing of engagement varies based on client needs and availability. Many expect to book their doula several months in advance —far earlier than many anticipate. This early booking ensures the relationship has time to develop properly before labor begins.

The initial meeting is crucial because it sets the tone for the entire birth experience. Both the doula and the family assess whether they're the right fit for each other. As Mary Riley explains in the episode , comfort and trust must be established before the doula begins official support.
"They have to walk away from this birth looking at each other and hopefully say, look at what we did together, because we have to parent and raise this child for the rest of our lives."

Mary Riley — Birth Doula with 39 years of experience, having supported over 2,500 births. Riley began her doula practice 39 years ago in the Hudson Valley after attending seven friends' births in one summer. She obtained her certification through weekend workshops and book learning, and has also worked as a midwife assistant at a freestanding birth center in Athens, collaborating throughout her career with home birth midwives.

During pregnancy itself, the relationship deepens through periodic in-person meetings —typically two to three visits—combined with responsive communication. This cadence allows the doula to understand the family's preferences, birth plans, and any concerns without overwhelming them with too much contact.

fc5cba5b0a.q: What is the biggest challenge of working as a doula?
fc5cba5b0a.a: Being on call is the hardest part of the job. It makes it difficult to plan personal activities and vacations because a birth can happen at any time, sometimes during scheduled time off. This lifestyle commitment means doulas must always be available, which requires backup doulas for emergency situations when the primary doula cannot be reached.
fc5cba5b0a.e: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula
f: Being on call means doulas must always be available for births , which makes it nearly impossible to plan personal activities or vacations with certainty. A birth can happen at any time, sometimes during scheduled time off, forcing doulas to maintain backup coverage and constantly put their own lives on hold.

The on-call lifestyle is fundamentally different from most careers. Unlike a job with set hours, doula work operates on the unpredictable rhythm of labor and delivery. A doula might spend anywhere from 10 to 50 hours during active labor support , with additional time needed for pre- and post-birth visits. This means the phone can ring at any moment—midnight, weekends, holidays—and the doula must be ready to respond.

As discussed in the episode , this unpredictability creates a cascade of practical problems. Booking flights for a vacation means risking cancellation fees. Planning family dinners becomes a gamble—you might have to leave halfway through. Even something as simple as a weekend getaway requires arranging backup doulas who can step in if you're unavailable . Without this safety net, you're trapped by the possibility of a client going into labor.

The challenge goes deeper than logistics. It's a psychological weight. You're never fully off duty. Your mind is always partially elsewhere, tracking your clients who are approaching their due dates. This constant state of alert can burn out even the most dedicated birth workers.
"They have to walk away from this birth looking at each other and hopefully say, look at what we did together, because we have to parent and raise this child for the rest of our lives."

Mary Riley — Birth Doula with 39 years of experience. Riley has supported over 2,500 births throughout her career, beginning after attending seven friends' births in one summer in the Hudson Valley. 9aff46e009.q: How do doulas work alongside hospital staff like nurses, midwives, and doctors?
9aff46e009.a: Years ago, Mary Riley faced significant resistance from hospital staff who did not recognize the doula role and even threw her out of hospitals. However, over time and through building trust with midwives and doctors, she developed collaborative relationships. Now she advocates for clients by learning each hospital's current rules, which change frequently, and helping clients communicate effectively with healthcare providers rather than approaching the birth as a confrontation. She emphasizes that all roles—doula, nurse, midwife, doctor—are important and work best as a team.
9aff46e009.e: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula
f: Doulas succeed in hospitals by abandoning confrontation and embracing collaboration as true team members with nurses, midwives, and doctors. Rather than advocating against hospital staff, they learn each facility's current protocols, help clients communicate effectively, and recognize that all roles—doula, nurse, midwife, doctor—are equally vital to a safe, supported birth.
From Resistance to Partnership: Building Hospital Trust

Early in her career, Mary Riley faced significant pushback. Hospital staff did not recognize the doula role, and she was occasionally thrown out of birthing rooms . But over time, through consistent presence and genuine respect for medical professionals, she transformed those relationships into genuine partnerships.

Today, Riley's approach reflects decades of learning what works. Rather than walking in with a fixed agenda or confrontational stance, she meets each hospital's unique culture and current rules —which change frequently—and helps her clients navigate those realities. As Riley explains in the episode , the shift happened when she stopped viewing hospital protocols as obstacles and started treating them as information that helps her serve clients better.
Advocacy Without Confrontation

A doula's role is to advocate for the client, but effective advocacy means communication, not conflict . Riley teaches her clients how to express their needs, preferences, and concerns directly to their medical team rather than positioning herself as an intermediary in a battle.

236e030bfd.q: What happens if a baby is born unexpectedly outside a hospital or birth center?
236e030bfd.a: Mary Riley has caught babies in emergency situations, including one recent birth on the Rhinecliffe Bridge where the mother's water broke in a car stuck in back-to-back traffic. She instructed the father to sing to calm himself and coached the mother to catch her own baby. The baby did not cry immediately, so Mary told the father to keep singing and had the mother place the baby skin-to-skin and pat the baby's back to clear the lungs. The baby then screamed and they proceeded to the birth center.
236e030bfd.e: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula
f: A doula's role in an emergency birth outside a hospital is to calm the parents, provide real-time coaching, and ensure the baby begins breathing safely . In one real case on the Rhinecliffe Bridge, Mary Riley instructed a father to sing while coaching the mother to catch her own baby, then guided them through keeping the infant warm and clearing its lungs until normal breathing resumed.

When labor begins unexpectedly outside a hospital or birth center, a doula becomes the steady voice in chaos. The immediate priority is managing the parents' panic—in Mary Riley's bridge delivery, she recognized that the father needed something concrete to do. Singing calmed him and, in turn, steadied the mother's focus on the task at hand.

Once the baby is born, skin-to-skin contact becomes critical for warmth and bonding. Riley instructed the mother to place the newborn directly against her chest and gently pat the baby's back to help clear the lungs and stimulate breathing. This simple physical action often triggers the baby's first cry, a vital sign that air is entering the lungs properly.

The entire emergency—from water breaking in traffic to safe transport—unfolded because one person knew how to translate medical knowledge into actionable steps that untrained parents could actually follow under extreme stress. As explored in this episode of How Much Can I Make? , this is exactly what separates panic births from managed ones.

f95c787e3c.q: How does a doula support partners and fathers during birth?

She ensures the partner understands his important role and gives him credit for managing sleep loss, stress, and learning how to advocate.

f: A doula keeps partners emotionally grounded and connected to the mother throughout labor , which calms everyone involved. She normalizes what the father is witnessing—especially the intensity of sounds and physical responses—and reassures him that his presence and support matter deeply to both his partner and the newborn.

Many partners and fathers arrive at birth with no frame of reference for what they are about to experience. They may feel uncertain about their role, anxious about the mother's pain, or even frightened by the raw intensity of labor itself. A doula addresses this directly and practically.

Mary Riley, who has supported over 2,500 births in her 39-year career, explains that her approach often includes physical reassurance of the partner —sometimes massaging the father's shoulders to help him relax. This small act keeps him present and engaged rather than overwhelmed or detached. At the same time, she continuously reinforces a key message: what is happening is normal and okay, even when it sounds or looks frightening to someone experiencing birth for the first time.

The doula also ensures the partner understands his specific, important role during labor and birth. Riley makes a point of giving the father genuine credit for the emotional and physical demands he manages—the sleep loss, the stress, the challenge of learning how to advocate for his partner's needs within a hospital or birth center setting. This recognition helps him feel like an active participant, not a bystander.
